passages.t: To the saints, the faithful in Christ Jesus
passages.happening:
The letter opens in the usual way: who it is from, who it is to, and a greeting.

“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus” (verse 1).

“Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
An apostle is someone sent with a message. Paul says he is one ‘by the will of God’, not by his own choice or anyone else's.

‘Saints’ means holy ones, people set apart for God. In the New Testament it is a word for all believers, not for a few especially good ones. The readers were mostly Gentiles who had once worshipped the gods of their cities. Now Paul calls them God's holy people. That is the first gift of the letter.

‘The faithful’ can mean those who believe, or those who are loyal. Both fit.

‘Grace and peace’ joins a Greek greeting and a Jewish one. Grace is God's free kindness. Peace, the Hebrew shalom, is wholeness, things put right. Both come from the Father and the Son together.
passages.ot:
God called Israel to be holy as he is holy: “Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19:2). He chose them, not because they were great, but because he loved them: “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples” (Deuteronomy 7:7).

Daniel saw a day when “the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom” (Daniel 7:18). Paul gives Gentile believers the name God gave his people Israel.
passages.hard:
Why do some Bibles mark ‘in Ephesus’ with a note?

The words ‘in Ephesus’ are missing from three of the earliest copies of the letter that survive: a papyrus from about AD 200, and the two great books of the 300s called Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, as first written. And the second-century teacher Marcion knew the letter as ‘To the Laodiceans’.

Many scholars think the letter was meant to travel from church to church in the province of Asia, with Ephesus as its chief stop, and that the place name was added in copies kept at Ephesus. Others think ‘in Ephesus’ is original and was dropped from some copies, and they point out that every early translation of the letter has it. These notes do not choose. The book page on Ephesians says more. On either view, the letter was written to Gentile believers in that region, and it speaks to every church.
passages.asks: Paul calls ordinary Gentile believers ‘saints’, holy ones. Ask whether you think of holiness as something for a few special people, or as what God has made of everyone who belongs to Christ. If you belong to him, what would change if you believed that God calls you holy?

passages.happening:
Paul bursts into praise. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms” (verse 3).

Then he names the blessings. God “chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence” (verse 4). In love “He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ” (verse 5). “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace” (verse 7).

God has made known “the mystery of His will” (verse 9): his plan “to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ” (verse 10). “In Him we were also chosen as God’s own” (verse 11).

And the readers too: “having heard and believed the word of truth—the gospel of your salvation—you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (verses 13-14). Three times the praise returns to a refrain: all of this is “to the praise of His glorious grace” (verse 6), “for the praise of His glory” (verse 12), “to the praise of His glory” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
In Greek, verses 3 to 14 are one long sentence, one of the longest in the New Testament. It is not tangled argument. It is praise that keeps overflowing. It is best read aloud.

It begins like a Jewish prayer. Many Jewish prayers open ‘Blessed be God’, praising him for what he has done. Paul uses that form and fills it with Christ.

Notice the shape. The Father chooses and plans (verses 3 to 6). The Son redeems and forgives (verses 7 to 12). The Spirit seals and guarantees (verses 13 and 14). Long before the creeds, Christian prayer was already shaped by the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

Several words come from daily life. Adoption was a Roman legal act that gave a person a new father and the full rights of an heir. Redemption was the price paid to free a slave or a captive. A seal was a mark pressed into wax or clay, showing who owned something and keeping it safe. A pledge was a first payment that promised the rest would follow. The Spirit is God's down payment on all that is to come.

‘In Christ’ or ‘in Him’ comes again and again. Every blessing is found in being joined to him.

And the plan is huge. God means to gather everything, in heaven and on earth, under Christ as head, like a sum brought together under one line. The church is the first sign of that.
passages.ot:
Israel blessed God for his acts again and again. “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel” (Luke 1:68) is how Zechariah began his song, in the manner of the psalms.

God's choosing is an Old Testament theme. Israel was told, “The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all peoples on the face of the earth” (Deuteronomy 7:6). And the reason was love, not merit (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). At Sinai God called Israel “My treasured possession” (Exodus 19:5); Paul's ‘God's own’ in verse 11 echoes the same idea.

Redemption takes the reader back to the exodus, when God “redeemed you from the house of slavery” (Deuteronomy 7:8).

And the promised Spirit is the Spirit of the prophets: “I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that God ‘chose us in Him before the foundation of the world’ and ‘predestined’ us? This is one of the places where faithful Christians have long disagreed. These notes set out the main readings and do not choose, as the notes on Romans 8 and 9 do not.

Reformed Christians read these words as God's loving choice, before creation, of particular people for salvation. They hold that the choice rests wholly on God's free mercy, not on anything foreseen in the people chosen, and that God surely brings those he chose to faith and to glory. They hear in verse 11 that God “works out everything by the counsel of His will”.

Arminian and Wesleyan Christians read the same words as God's choice of all who are in Christ. They note that believers are chosen ‘in Him’, and hold that God, knowing beforehand who would freely trust him, chose them in Christ. They point to verses such as “who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4).

Others, in both traditions, stress that Paul speaks of ‘us’: God chose a people in Christ, and each person comes into that chosen people by faith. They note that Paul goes on to speak of the Gentiles' coming in (verses 13-14).

All agree on what these verses are for. They are praise. Paul does not write them to make anyone anxious. He writes so that believers will know that their salvation began in God's love before time, not in their own effort, and so that they will be humble and secure. All agree too that God's choosing is ‘in Him’, in Christ, and that it was ‘in love’ (verses 4-5). The site's Honest Answer, ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose him?’, sets out each case.

If you are afraid that you are not chosen, hear the invitation of Jesus: “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul's first response to God's choosing is not argument but praise. Ask whether your thoughts about God's choice lead you to praise or to worry. And read verses 3 to 14 aloud, slowly. Which of the blessings named there do you most need to hear is true of you today?

passages.t: A prayer to know the hope, the riches and the power
passages.happening:
Paul tells them he prays for them. He has heard of their faith and love, and he keeps giving thanks (verses 15-16).

He asks that God “may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him” (verse 17). “I ask that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened, so that you may know the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe” (verses 18-19).

That power is the power God used when he raised Christ from the dead “and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly realms, far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named” (verses 20-21). “And God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
Paul does not pray that they will get more blessings. He prays that they will see the ones they already have.

‘The eyes of your heart’ is a striking phrase. In the Bible the heart is not only feelings. It is the centre of a person, where thinking, choosing and loving happen. Paul prays that their inner sight will be opened.

He names three things to see. The hope God's call gives. The riches of God's inheritance: either the inheritance believers receive, or, as many read it, God's own people as his treasured inheritance. And God's power toward believers.

How great is that power? It is the power that raised Jesus from the dead. The readers lived in a city famous for magic, where people bought charms and spells to protect themselves from spirits and powers. Paul says that Christ has been raised ‘far above’ every such power, and that the power at work in believers is the power of the resurrection.

The resurrection here is not a picture or a feeling. It is what God did to the dead body of Jesus: he raised him and seated him in honour. The church confesses it as the ground of all its hope.

‘Head’ and ‘body’ are Paul's picture of Christ and the church. The church does not own Christ. Christ fills the church, and through it, in the end, he fills everything.
passages.ot:
Paul reads two psalms. In Psalm 110 God says to the king, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1). The New Testament reads this psalm again and again as speaking of Christ's rising and reign (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:34-36; Hebrews 1:13).

Psalm 8 marvels that God gave human beings rule over his works: “You have placed everything under his feet” (Psalm 8:6). Paul sees that calling fulfilled in Jesus, the true human, raised and reigning.

And the ‘spirit of wisdom’ recalls Isaiah's promise of the Messiah, on whom would rest “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isaiah 11:2).
passages.asks: Paul prays that the eyes of their hearts will be opened. Try praying his prayer for someone you love, by name. Then ask what you most need to see: the hope you have, the worth you have to God, or the power that raised Jesus at work in you. And ask what powers you fear, and whether you believe Christ is above them.
